Public, mandatory moderation log for every subverse is now partially implemented.

Public modlog is accessible for every subverse at subversename/modlog/deleted.

For example, to access the moderator submission removal log for subverse /v/test, go to https://voat.co/v/test/modlog/deleted.

For now, moderators can not give a reason when deleting a submission. This feature is coming, but it may take some time. All moderator-removed submissions will automatically be added to /deleted log, and accessible with original URL, title and submission text. For technical reasons, original author will be unknown, but this is something we can improve and implement later on. The important thing is that moderator who removed the submission will be listed, along with timestamp of removed submission and original submission with comments.

This log will only show submissions which were removed by a moderator.

Please try it out and comment here if you find anything unusual. Do you like this feature? Hate it? Leave a comment. Or don't. I'm not the boss of you.

Edit: logging starts from the posting time of this announcement.

I am all for transparency. Which is why I want to address a potential problem before it crops up. That is: private personal information.

When a moderator removes a post because it contains the real name and phone number or address of some other user, would that still show up in the log?

Or if a removed post contains the phone number and address for a congressman?

Or perhaps the twitter/youtube page for a reddit user who uses the same username on both reddit and twitter/youtube?

Or an article in a widely viewed service like kotaku that contains the real name of some famous voat or reddit user?

What about a removed post that has the facebook page for a public figure, or a person doing something dumb on a youtube video?

Some of this stuff I think should remain hidden, to the best of the website's ability (nothing can be removed from the internet if there's enough attention focused on it), and some of it I think should not be - and one or two I am uncertain on.

So what do you think should happen in those circumstances?

I don't know if there are any laws against these things, if you need a special user agreement CYA thing to be able to wash your hands of any inability to stop it, or if there's some automated way of flagging something as personal information and having it hidden to be reviewed by you or another admin, etc.

I think it would be good if we decide what the approach to things like this will be before they happen, to make sure that we don't end up having a shitty emergency solution put in place that cripples the value of the public mod logs.

I have some concerns with this.

With my experience moderating large subreddits, there are some pretty good reasons why moderators might want the mod log to be private at times.

When it comes to removal of submissions, if the removal is public then it isn't REALLY removed is it? It's still there, providing whatever moderate quantity of traffic regularly views the public modlog and there's still a point to spamming the service as a result of that moderate traffic generated. This kind of thing would create a larger quantity of things mods will need to remove.

This won't be visible now, it won't be visible until the service scales up to the kinds of sizes you see from 50-150k subscriber levels of subreddits, but it WILL become a large problem.

There are further reasons as to why reddit hasn't implemented this feature as a part of reddit when it wouldn't be particularly difficult - Moderators can already use other tools to get it to work if they wish, voluntarily at their own will. If reddit were to add this feature as something mods can voluntarily make public or not then ALL subreddits that choose not to would automatically get attacked for it.

Just a few thoughts you guys should consider with the future of this kind of implementation. I don't support making mod logs public, it's not necessary. Instead of attacking mods for what they may or may not remove and the biases they hold it would be more prudent to look at other issues reddit has with moderators, such as inactive mods holding positions that don't actually do anything purely for the ego value of being in such positions, and subreddits with woefully small mod teams.

One particular fear I have with this is mob mentality. When subreddits get VERY large the sub gets out of the control of the moderators (who technically own the subreddit). The community starts to view it as owned by them and various issues occur such as moderators getting hell for removing things the community likes that the moderators don't want as part of their community. This gets into a whole other theorhetical area of who owns subverses, on reddit the moderators are treated as owning their communities, which is the right approach really given that they're often the creators of that community and guiding light that led to its growth.

I have an alternate suggestion - Instead of making something mandatory for all subverses, make something mandatory only for subverses that would make up a sort of "front page" like the defaults of reddit. I've always felt that subreddits accepted in becoming defaults should have a higher standard of control and management than other subreddits, standardised by the admins. Features like this could be mandatory for inclusion in such.

I think moderators need softer tools in addition to deleting as well. Tools like freezing voats, and locking from further comments (both for submissions and comment trees) as well as hiding comments as default. Nothing should be deleted unless it's illegal content and all moderation should be required to list a reason why action was taken.

If a submission or comment breaks the subverse rules it should only be locked, frozen, and/or hidden by default. I really can't think of a reason why you'd want to delete content unless it's illegal or you're a cancerous and corrupt mod. Still there will always be bad mods. This is why it would also be great if users could filter out actions taken by specific mods. This way if the integrity of a mod is in question, a user can simply uncheck them from the moderator que. Once this is done all content hidden by them will automatically be shown and it would be amazing if frozen voats and locked topics would be unlocked for those who have removed the moderator's actions from their view. New posts/voats after a lock/freeze would be unavailable to those who still trust the mod, but those unchecking the mod's actions would see new posts and updated voat tallies.

Thank you for implementing the beginnings of a public moderation log. I think this is a really important step to ensuring transparency.

There will probably come a time where something illegal sneaks into the title of something that is removed, and the illegal content will still be stored in the moderation log. My suggestion is that, in preparation for that eventuality, you make it so that admins (but not moderators) can remove/edit out PI in modlog titles, or only include the first few characters of a submission title as well as the OP's username (and, of course, the username of the mod who deleted the post) to prevent illegal content actually being in the title itself.
